item.title: Munich Re CFO: Retro optional, no current need for cat bonds. We underwrite to keep the risk
item.description: “So any form of ceding externally risk, that we do as part of our wider retrocession programme, I’d say is a somewhat optional activity for us.” Buchanan continued, “We underwrite risks very much with the conviction that we underwrite them in such a way that we can keep them for ourselves. Speaking this morning during an earnings call, Munich Re’s CFO Andrew Buchanan gave the clearest explanation for why the global reinsurance company has reduced its retrocessional protection considerably, saying the company puts the effort into underwriting so it can keep the risk and has the financial strength to warehouse it. “Certainly at the current point in the market, with rates still being adequate, we are quite happy to retain risk and to earn the full profit margin for risk-bearing ourselves.

item.title: Colombia secures parametric insurance for smallholder farmers, assisted by IDF, UNDP, BMZ
item.description: The Colombian government has contracted five parametric agricultural insurance policies to provide smallholder farmers with coverage against drought and excess rainfall, utilising a solution developed by the Insurance Development Forum (IDF), UNDP, and Germany’s BMZ via the InsuResilience Solutions Fund (ISF). According to the announcement, the parametric policies developed under the Tripartite Agreement, a public-private partnership, will directly cover 14,402 smallholder farmers, benefitting up to 41,600 people across their households in five departments: Sucre, Córdoba, Cundinamarca, Meta and Chocó. As mentioned, the five parametric agricultural insurance policies were delivered through the Tripartite Agreement Programme, a public-private partnership between the Insurance Development Forum (IDF), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), through the InsuResilience Solutions Fund (ISF).

item.title: TSR lowers hurricane season forecast as sub-tropical Atlantic looking less favourable
item.description: Tropical Storm Risk (TSR) has now lowered its forecast for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season at an update today, citing “conditions in the sub-tropical Atlantic looking less favourable than as appeared to be a month ago.” Recall that, in its April forecast, Tropical Storm Risk (TSR) lowered its previous long-range forecast to call for 12 named tropical storms, 5 hurricanes and just 1 major hurricane for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, with expected accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) of 66. TSR has lowered its forecast from early July due to conditions in the sub-tropical Atlantic looking less favourable than as appeared to be a month ago.” On the ACE Index, TSR now says it sees a 0% probability of the 2026 season being in the upper tercile (>156)), a 26% likelihood of being in the middle tercile (75 to 156)) and a 74% chance of being lower tercile with ACE below 75. But, with the season passing and approaching its accepted peak, TSR now feels tropical conditions are less conducive to storm formation again, reducing the figures in today’s forecast update for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.

item.title: RGA’s net income climbs 157% to $462m in Q2’26

Adjusted operating income stood at $586 million, up 86% from $315 million in Q2’25. Investment income for the quarter, excluding spread-based businesses, increased 10.3% year on year, primarily due to a larger average invested asset base.

item.title: P&C environment remains attractive, no acceleration in rate softening at July 1: Munich Re CEO
item.description: Christoph Jurecka, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of reinsurance giant Munich Re, has underlined the company’s ability to walk away from business where pricing is viewed as inadequate, but added that the P&C market is still attractive as the volume of business written by the reinsurer at the July renewals fell by 9.1%. Alongside its results, the carrier disclosed its July 1 reinsurance renewal outcome amid the softening environment, revealing a negative volume change of more than 9% to €2.1 billion, with a risk-adjusted price decline of -5.5%, comprised of a nominal price change of -4.4% and a business mix effect of -1.1%. In other lines of business, Munich Re cut back in Specialty lines and Casualty XL driven by active cycle management, but notes that profitability remains attractive.

item.title: AXA XL to Acquire Corporate Intelligence and Cybersecurity Consultancy, S-RM
item.description: AXA XL announced it has entered into an agreement to acquire S-RM, the London-based specialist corporate intelligence and cybersecurity consultancy — raising its shareholding from approximately 49% to 100% ownership. item.title: Oil-Related Materials Claims Exposure Varies Broadly Across US
item.description: According to the report , claims costs for various materials are broadly varying, depending on what the area of the country: vinyl siding claims are most impacted across parts of the Midwest, while roofing-related costs are big in storm-prone southern states. Oil prices are giving claims costs a hit, and depending on the part of the country, the exposure for replacement and repair costs of roofing, synthetic flooring or vinyl siding may be considerable and vary broadly, a new report shows. Verisk identified three “petroleum-intensive material categories” that account for the largest share of oil-related claims exposure.

item.title: New Database Shows 6.5 Million Americans Face Landslide Risks — and Where They Live
item.description: The database, developed by University of Washington researchers, rates 128 million buildings by landslide susceptibility, and uses socioeconomic data to assess residents’ vulnerability to the dangers and disruptions caused by landslides. According to the analysis, roughly 6.5 million people live in landslide-prone regions; most of those people are concentrated in Appalachia and along the West Coast. The new Landslide Exposure Database, or LED, is the first resource to map building-level landslide risk for the entire US.

item.title: NOAA Maintains Forecast for Below-Normal Atlantic Hurricane Season
item.description: Nearly halfway through the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, NOAA’s prediction of below-normal activity in the Atlantic basin remains unchanged. NOAA forecasters predict a 75% chance of below-normal activity, with a 20% chance of a near-normal season, and just a 5% chance of above-normal activity. In the Atlantic basin, a typical hurricane season will find 14 named storms, with seven becoming hurricanes, including three major hurricanes.

item.title: Climate Change Made Canada’s Forests Much More Likely to Burn: Report
item.description: The planet’s warming had a strong influence on destructive wildfires in Canada that have raged across Ontario and the Northwest Territories since late June, making the extreme fire weather that fueled them at least twice as likely, according to a report published Thursday by World Weather Attribution. To quantify the effect of climate change on Canada’s wildfires, the study’s authors leveraged observation data and climate models to compare how the events would have unfolded in a world without warming. The change is even more stark in the Northwest Territories: There, a week of fire weather as extreme as this year’s — which would occur once-a-decade without global warming — is now estimated to return every two years.

item.title: Why Multifamily Owners’ Safety Investments Aren’t Showing Up in Their Premiums
item.description: Multifamily owners have spent years hardening properties, but most carriers still lack a consistent way to price that resilience into premiums. Multifamily owners have spent the last several years pouring capital into resilience, in the form of hardened roofs, backup power and fortified building envelopes, to name a few. Here, Brandon Tobman, CEO of GetCovered, a risk and compliance platform of multifamily property owners, covers why per-unit insurance costs have climbed sharply since 2020, why proven resilience data (like FORTIFIED-roof outcomes after Hurricane Sally) still isn't reaching underwriting models, and what a documentation-first standard could look like for carriers ready to close the resilience-underwriting gap.
